opus-5.5.text:
Right now a lot of the friction in adopting these models for software engineering isn't that they can't write code. It's that they're kind of a weird, half-useful intern. They can autocomplete a function or write a small script, but you as the engineer have to do all the scaffolding: break the problem down, feed in the right context, check every line, stitch it back into the codebase. Integrating that into a real workflow is a ton of work, and companies have to change their processes to get value out of a tool that's only partially competent.

So the counterintuitive thing is that more capability can actually make adoption *easier*, not harder. Once the model is good enough to act like a drop-in remote worker, it can onboard the way a new hire would. It reads the codebase, looks at the Slack threads and the docs, picks up a ticket, works on it for hours or days, runs the tests, and comes back with a pull request. At that point you don't need to redesign your whole organization around the AI. You just plug it in like another engineer. The integration cost collapses.

A lot of what I call "unhobbling" is about this: moving from a chatbot you have to babysit to an agent that can use a computer, keep long-horizon context, and correct its own mistakes. The intermediate stage, where models are useful but need a lot of hand-holding, is actually the hardest to adopt. Crossing that threshold to "it can just do the job" is what I'd expect to unlock a sudden jump in uptake, especially in software, where the work is already digital and the feedback loops, like compiling and testing, are right there.

r001.rationale: The response says intermediate models need substantial human scaffolding, context-setting, checking, and workflow changes, making them hard to adopt.

r002.rationale: It describes a capable model handling a task and returning a pull request, but does not clearly state that it can do the work without requiring a human software engineer.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing people miss is that adoption isn't really bottlenecked by how smart the model is on a single task. It's bottlenecked by what I'd call the schlep. Right now, if you want to actually get value out of these models in a real software engineering workflow, somebody has to do an enormous amount of work on top of them. You have to build the scaffolding, you have to figure out the tool integrations, you have to wire up the context about your codebase, you have to babysit it when it goes off the rails. And that's expensive. That's a bunch of senior engineers spending months just to make the thing reliable enough that you'd trust it.

And the reason extra capability matters is that it eats the schlep. A model that's a bit smarter can figure out your codebase on its own instead of needing you to hand-curate the context. It can recover from its own mistakes instead of needing a human to catch them. It can use the tools you already have instead of needing a bespoke harness built around it. So you go from "we need a six-month internal project to make this work" to "an engineer tries it on Tuesday and it just works."

I think of it a bit like the difference between a brilliant intern who needs everything explained and a mid-level engineer who you can just hand a ticket to. The intern might even be smarter on some narrow benchmark, but the mid-level engineer is the one who actually gets adopted, because the integration cost on the human side drops to almost nothing.

And this is why I think adoption could be really nonlinear. It's not that each increment of capability gives you a proportional increment of usage. It's that at some threshold, the model crosses from "needs a team to deploy" to "drop-in," and at that point every company with a GitHub repo can use it basically overnight. The last few years, people have looked at the slow enterprise rollout and concluded diffusion is inherently slow. I think that's wrong. It's been slow because the models weren't quite good enough to make the integration trivial, and that's a capability problem, not an inherent feature of how organizations work.

r001.rationale: It describes substantial scaffolding, integration, codebase-context setup, and babysitting as costly work that makes software-engineering adoption difficult.

r002.rationale: It says a more capable model could handle context, recover from mistakes, and use existing tools with less setup, but does not clearly state that it could perform software-engineering work without a human software engineer.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that there’s a big difference between being able to do a task with a lot of supervision and being able to do it reliably on your own. If the model writes some code, but you have to explain every detail, give it the right context, and then spend a bunch of time finding its mistakes, that limits how useful it is. You have to reorganize your workflow around its weaknesses.

With more capability, you can delegate something much closer to a whole task: here’s the bug, go figure out what’s causing it, make the change, run the tests. The model can deal with the ambiguities and recover when something goes wrong. That makes adoption much simpler because the human doesn’t have to supply all that scaffolding.

So I wouldn’t treat capability and adoption as entirely separate things, where you first get the technology and then wait for organizations to catch up. Some of what looks like an adoption problem is actually a capability problem. Make the model reliable enough to take work off someone’s plate, and the incentive to use it becomes much stronger.

r001.rationale: It says less capable models require detailed instructions and context, plus time spent finding mistakes and reorganizing workflows, which limits usefulness and adoption.

r002.rationale: It describes delegating a whole task while the model handles ambiguity and errors, but does not clearly say the work can be done without a human software engineer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s this intuition that adoption has to lag capabilities by many years, because organizations are slow to change. And that’s true to some extent. But a lot of what looks like an adoption problem is actually a capabilities problem.

Suppose the model can write a function, but you have to give it very precise instructions, supply all the context, and then spend a bunch of time checking and fixing what it wrote. Integrating that into your workflow takes effort. You have to figure out which tasks it’s good at, how to break them down, when to trust it. The human is still doing all this management.

If instead you can hand it an issue and it goes off, understands the codebase, implements the change, runs the tests, and comes back with something that works, adoption becomes much easier. You’re delegating a task in a way you already know how to do.

So extra capability can substitute for a lot of the work people imagine has to happen around the model. The model can learn your tools, deal with the messy context, and ask you a question when it’s stuck. You still need verification and accountability, but the amount of organizational adaptation required can fall quite dramatically as the systems get better.

r001.rationale: It describes the effort of supplying context, giving precise instructions, checking and fixing outputs, and managing the model as work that makes adoption harder.

r002.rationale: It says a capable model could take an issue, implement a change, and run tests, but retains human verification and accountability; it does not clearly state that software engineering work would no longer require a human software engineer.
